title: Strat Chat - 'We Do' Checks for Understanding
author: Mutually Assured Instruction
summary: This Strat Chat installment from Mutually Assured Instruction offers two concrete techniques for the 'We Do' phase of a gradual-release lesson, aimed at teachers whose checks for understanding have gone stale from overuse of the same one or two routines. The first, Example Problem Pairs, pairs a teacher's worked example with an immediate, structurally similar independent problem, leaving the worked example visible as a scaffold so stronger students can lean on it less. The author explains how a math-teaching colleague's routine practice transferred surprisingly well into Humanities subjects wherever the curriculum applies the same kind of knowledge repeatedly across different content. The second technique, 'Write It/Say It/Do It Again Better,' borrowed from Natalie Wexler's The Writing Revolution, insists that feedback is inert unless students act on it immediately by redoing their response, rather than simply hearing whole-class feedback and moving on. Both strategies come with explicit cautions: worked examples must stay tightly parallel to avoid adding cognitive load, and revised responses must be checked, or students may simply practice new misconceptions more fluently. The piece closes by framing the whole 'We Do' phase as a balance between over-scaffolding, which prevents independent thinking, and premature independence, which leaves students without the practice they need.
points: Example Problem Pairs combine the worked-example effect with the confidence of independent practice: the teacher solves one problem aloud, then students immediately attempt a similar problem with the worked example left visible as a scaffold.
The technique, borrowed from math teaching, transfers well to Humanities subjects wherever a curriculum's knowledge point is applied the same way across varying content.

'Write It/Say It/Do It Again Better,' adapted from Natalie Wexler's The Writing Revolution, treats feedback as incomplete unless students immediately redo the response, closing a loop whole-class feedback alone leaves open.

Both strategies carry a 'teacher beware': worked examples must stay tightly parallel to avoid raising cognitive load, and revised 'better' responses must actually be checked, or students risk practicing new misconceptions.
The author frames the We Do phase as a balancing act between too much scaffolding and too much independence, positioning both strategies as tools for holding that middle ground.
quotes: An example problem pair is something I only began to utilize this year after having a discussion with a math teaching colleague and realizing that it was a tool they used constantly which I was not realizing had so much potential in the Humanities subjects I teach.

The example problem pair pairs the power of the worked example effect with the feeling of independent success which comes from a You Do. Almost a You Do with training wheels on as the teacher thinks aloud and solves a question step by step on one side of the board before asking students to complete a similar, yet slightly different problem on the other side with their example remaining on the board as a scaffold to work from.

A check for understanding is all about feedback, both for the teacher and the student. But feedback without action is just noise. Unless we do something with the feedback, then it's just empty words to the benefit of nobody.

First you need to conduct any other check for understanding where students either write, say or do something. Then the teacher provides feedback (hopefully constructive) before asking the students to write, say or do their response again, but better!
The example problems need to be alike in how the knowledge is applied otherwise the worked example could potentially mislead students or even add further to their cognitive load.
Too much scaffolding and students haven't had to think hard enough to move to independence. Too much independence and students will not have had the practice they need to know where to start.
